title: A Change of Course in Wastewater Treatment: From an Underground Town Relay to Treatment at Each Home
part1:
You flush the toilet. You use water in the kitchen, bathroom, and laundry. The household wastewater produced each time has often entered sewers running underground through towns and headed to large treatment plants. In a sense, it is a long-distance relay for wastewater.

But now, there is a movement to reconsider the course of this relay. The key question is whether homes are close together or spread out.

In areas where homes are densely packed, many homes can share pipes and treatment plants, so centralized treatment, such as public sewers, may be more economical. In contrast, in areas where homes are spread out, treatment tanks for each home may be more advantageous. This does not mean that treatment tanks are always cheaper. Costs must be compared for each area, including construction, maintenance, and existing facilities.

One reason behind this is the decline in population and the aging of facilities. The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism explains that lower income from sewer fees due to population decline and other factors, along with higher costs for rebuilding and replacing aging facilities, will make it harder to run sewer services.
part2:
In addition, the ministry estimates that the cost of maintaining and replacing sewer systems will rise from about 0.8 trillion yen in fiscal 2018 to about 1.3 trillion yen in fiscal 2048. This is an estimated increase to about 1.6 times the current level. It is important to note that this is not a fixed future, but an estimate of what may happen.

Kitakata City in Fukushima Prefecture reviewed its wastewater treatment plan because maintenance costs are expected to rise as facilities age and need to be replaced, while fee income is expected to fall as the population declines. The city says that areas outside centralized treatment areas will become individual treatment areas using combined-treatment tanks, and that it will provide an additional subsidy for the cost of installing the tanks. In other words, the plan is not to remove all sewers, but to change the way treatment areas will be divided in the future.
part3:
The main actors, combined-treatment tanks, treat not only human waste from toilets but also household wastewater from kitchens, bathrooms, and laundry. They are small treatment facilities for each home that use the work of microorganisms.

However, installing one does not mean that it can simply be left to run automatically. People responsible for treatment tanks must have them inspected and cleaned. For small household tanks, maintenance inspections are basically required at least once every four months, and cleaning is required at least once a year. The number of times varies depending on the system and the number of people served. Legal inspections are also required separately.

The future of wastewater treatment is not about whether sewers or treatment tanks win or lose. It is about choosing a new route for wastewater based on the town’s population and the way its homes are arranged. This kind of change in course is now beginning.
in_one_line: Population decline and aging sewers are prompting a shift from centralized treatment to tanks at individual homes.
